name: Fort Dearborn — officers' quarters

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS THE FORT'S, NOT THIS BUILDING'S. No source reached dates any individual building inside Fort Dearborn. It opens with the rebuild of 1816 (Andreas; Wentworth quoting the Adjutant-General, 'the post was reoccupied about June, 1816 ... Nothing is on file respecting the rebuilding of the Fort') and closes with the demolition of the fort's principal structures in the summer of 1856 (Andreas). What carries the scene date is the middle: this building is drawn standing on the 1830 plan and described standing in Hubbard's 1827 walk round the inside, and the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

placement.position_note: READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN. Position in pixels on the plate Andreas reproduces at vol. 1 p. 113, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel (the scale derivation is on fort_dearborn_palisade and in docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md section 3), rotated to the sheet's true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221. Carry +/-20 percent on the offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself. The facade bearing is the fort's 8-degree rotation plus the side of the parade this building faces, because every range in this fort fronts the parade. Hubbard, 1827: 'The old officers' quarters built of logs on the west, and within the pickets'. Andreas: 'The officers' quarters were on the west side'. The 1830 plan draws a long range against the west wall, and that range is this building.
placement.symbolic_location: Inside the west wall of Fort Dearborn, fronting east onto the parade.

footprint.note: TWO READINGS THAT DO NOT AGREE, AND THIS RECORD TAKES THE STATED ONE. The 1855 key gives 'the Officers' Quarters, B (wood, about 30x60 ft,)' - 9.14 x 18.29 m, which is the polygon here. The 1830 plan draws the west range about 30 ft deep and about 80 ft long at the scale this project derives, so the two agree on the depth to within 3 percent and disagree on the length by nearly 40 percent. THE STATED FIGURE WINS, and the reasoning is worth writing down because it decides several records: the scale that would overrule it was itself calibrated on the other stated figure in the same caption, so using it to correct that caption's second number is close to circular. What that costs is legible - the modelled building is about 6 m shorter than the plan draws its range - and it is why this footprint is inferred while the commandant's is documented. If the 1830 plan is right the officers were housed in an 80 ft range; if the 1855 caption is right they were in a 60 ft one; nothing reached settles it.

kind.note: Named as the officers' quarters by Hubbard in 1827, by Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort, and by the 1855 photograph key.

construction.note: Hubbard, standing in the fort in 1827: 'The old officers' quarters built of logs on the west'. The 1855 key says 'wood', which is the same claim less precisely. A CORRECTION TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOSSIER: docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 1.2 reads Andreas as giving brick officers' quarters on the west and flags a conflict with the 1855 key. Andreas's page 84 states no material for them at all, and his page 264 - Hubbard's own words - says logs. The conflict was a misreading; the two sources agree.

stories.note: RECONSTRUCTED STILL, BUT NO LONGER 'NOT ATTESTED ANYWHERE' (T-3124). That phrase was stale. Hubbard, describing the fort as he first saw it in October 1818, says 'The officers' quarters were outside of the pickets, fronting east on the parade, and was a two-story building of hewn logs' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358). That is earlier evidence for two storeys than anything this note used to rest on. IT DOES NOT PROMOTE THE GRADE, for two reasons the same book supplies. First, Hubbard contradicts himself on where the building stood: page 36 puts the officers' quarters OUTSIDE the pickets, while his 1827 walk round the fort puts 'The old officers' quarters, built of logs, on the west, and within the pickets' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 205, printed p. 167, committed text lines 7612-7613), which is where the 1830 plan draws this range; the source record lists the contradiction as something it does not supply. Second, nothing says the two-storey building of 1818 is the same range that stood in July 1835 rather than an earlier one — the post stood ungarrisoned from October 1823 to October 1828 and again from May 1831 to June 1832 (Hubbard's own table, printed p. 35), and no building inside it is dated. So the 1818 sentence is carried forward only CONDITIONALLY, on the reading that p. 36's 'outside' is a slip and the range never changed. The count's older argument still stands beside it: this range and the commandant's quarters are the two buildings the 1855 photograph shows as 'the principal buildings of the Fort', and a single-storey log range would not read as one of two principal buildings beside a two-storey brick one. That photograph is a diagnostic only, twenty years after the scene date, and no camera has been solved on it as a matched view of July 1835.

wall_height_m.note: No height is attested. 4.8 m is two storeys of log wall at period course counts. The number inherits the storey count's weakness above it.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal form for a log range of this period and plan.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, and it is inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. A 60 ft officers' range through Chicago winters needs a stack at each end by type. The COUNT is the inference; position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md.

gallery.note: AN UPPER PIAZZA, BUILT AS A RECONSTRUCTION ON HUBBARD'S EARLIER TEXT, NOT AS ATTESTATION (T-3124). Hubbard, of the officers' quarters he saw in 1818: 'A piazza extended along the entire front on a line with the floor of the second story, and was reached by stairs on the outside' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358). It is rendered with the fort archetype's existing two-level gallery (gallery_storeys 2): an open ground level of posts under an upper walk at the second floor, a rail along its front, and a canopy from the main eave. THE GRADE STAYS RECONSTRUCTED because the same unresolved questions the storey count carries apply here with more force: Hubbard puts that building OUTSIDE the pickets on p. 36 and the log officers' quarters WITHIN them on the west on p. 167, and nothing identifies the 1818 building with this 1835 range, so the piazza's continuity into the 1831-1835 garrison is conditional on both. THE PRIOR REFUSAL IS KEPT ON THE RECORD: until T-3124 this attribute read false with the note that nothing said the 1816 fort's ranges had galleries, that Whistler's 1808 'Galliaries fronting the parade' belonged to the first fort, and that John H. Kinzie called the two forts 'differently constructed'. That was written without p. 36, and it is the alternative a visitor would have seen had the text not been read. EVERY DIMENSION IS RECONSTRUCTED: the 2.1 m reach, post sections and rhythm, deck, rail, pales and canopy fall are the helper's choices (docs/LIBERTIES.md L-first-fort-double-galleries and L-second-fort-officers-piazza-3124); Hubbard gives none. THE OUTSIDE STAIRS ARE NOT MODELLED: he attests them but not where they ran or which way they climbed, and the helper invents no stair. The 1855 photograph is diagnostic only and is not a matched July 1835 view.

gallery_storeys.note: Two levels because Hubbard puts the piazza 'on a line with the floor of the second story' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358), so the walk is the upper one and the ground level under it is open. Graded reconstructed, not inferred, because the identification of Hubbard's building with this range is unresolved (see gallery and stories). The upper floor sits at the existing 2.4 m storey line of the unchanged 4.8 m wall; the helper's other dimensions are reconstructed.

face_openings.note: THE OLD LAYOUT, WRITTEN DOWN, NOT A NEW READING (T-3124). These are exactly the rectangles the archetype's procedural default already built on this range — five bays to the parade front with the ground-floor centre bay given to a door, four to the back, each storey's sills at 0.30 and heads at 0.72 of its 2.4 m — declared explicitly so that the upper piazza's supports can be set clear of them. Nothing moves: every opening stands where it stood before, and the left and right gable ends keep no openings, as before. No picture or text gives this building's openings; Hubbard's room list (kitchen, dining and store rooms below, one large room above) is not a fenestration, and every rectangle remains reconstructed.

function.note: Quarters for the post's subordinate officers. In 1827, with the fort ungarrisoned, Hubbard found them occupied by Russel E. Heacock 'and one other American family' - which is evidence about 1827, not about 1835.

occupants.value: Assistant Surgeon Philip Maxwell and Lieut. James Allen, and the rest of the post's subordinate officers unnamed
occupants.note: NAMED, NOT PROMOTED (T-1348). This block read 'subordinate officers of the garrison' and claimed the same thing it claims now; what it did not do was say who. Two men in this dataset are commissioned officers of the United States Army printed at Chicago across 1 July 1835. Philip Maxwell is Andreas's assistant surgeon, on duty at the post from 3 February 1833 to the abandonment, and hh_maxwell_philip already carries this building as its lives_at. James Allen is the papers': army officer and engineer, printed at the Democrat of 25 March 1834 and of 13 August 1834 and at the American of 18 July 1835 — seventeen days after the scene date, which is what makes his household present rather than uncertain. NO SOURCE PUTS EITHER MAN IN THIS BUILDING, so the grade does not move: the Army quartered a lieutenant and a post surgeon in the subordinate officers' quarters and this dataset holds one. ELEVEN OTHER NAMES WERE RULED OUT, each for a stated clause — a militia colonel, a man on the town poll roll, a soldier's trade read once in January 1834 and never again. The whole adjudication is docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn_garrison_1835.md. The enlisted strength stays unwritten and unnumbered here (T-1349), and Hubbard's 1827 civilian tenants belong to the years when there were no troops.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS ONLY 26 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

residents.name: The post surgeon's household
residents.why: A commissioned officer of the garrison lodged in the officers' quarters. The building is in the dataset and the practice is universal for a post of this kind; no source puts this man in this building, hence inferred. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR `lives_at` AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW `hh_maxwell_philip#lives_at`, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start (T-1273)

persons.name: Dr Philip Maxwell
persons.note: A GARRISON OFFICER WHOSE TOUR BRACKETS THE SCENE DATE AT BOTH ENDS - 3 February 1833 to 29 December 1836 - which makes him one of the few people in the dataset whose presence on 1 July 1835 is a matter of record rather than of inference. Born at Guilford, Windham Co., Vt., 3 April 1799; practised at Sackett's Harbor, N.Y., and sat in the New York legislature before his appointment. He was a witness to the Indian treaty of 26 September 1833.

residents.research_note: THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THIS PARCEL WHOSE PRESENCE NEEDS NO ARGUMENT, and the one that identifies a missing building. Everything about Maxwell is dated: birth, appointment, arrival, treaty witness, departure. What is not in the dataset is the room he worked in. THE GARRISON IS UNDER-REPRESENTED HERE ON PURPOSE. Fort Dearborn on 1 July 1835 was an occupied post under Major John Greene with an enlisted company, and this parcel writes only the two officers the sources name and date. Every private soldier is a documented human being whom no source in this dataset names, and turning a muster strength into person records is derived-phase work with a muster roll, not something to guess at now.

citations.citation: Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, Pa-pa-ma-ta-be, "The Swift Walker", with an Introduction by Caroline M. McIlvaine, Librarian of the Chicago Historical Society (Chicago: R. R. Donnelley & Sons Company, The Lakeside Press, Christmas 1911) — The Lakeside Classics. Read in full for its Chicago material before 1836: the front matter, McIlvaine's Introduction (pages ix-xxvii), and Hubbard's own narrative at pages 27-41, 135-138, 141-144, 153-159, 165-174 and 178-182. Hubbard's letter of 25 July 1827, printed as a note at page 174, is a separate source record.

transcribes.work: Hubbard's own autobiographical narrative — his engagement with the American Fur Company at Montreal and Mackinaw, the voyage of September 1818, his first entry into Chicago on 1 October 1818, the fort and its neighbours as he first saw them, the Chicago portage and Mud Lake, Hubbard's Trail, the trading posts of the Illinois River, and the Winnebago Scare of 1827 — ending abruptly at November 1830
transcribes.date: Written in the 1880s; printed 1888 and again 1911. Describes 1818-1830.
transcribes.note: A participant's recollection at more than fifty years' distance, and the rung most of this reading sits on. It is a recollection and not a record: the Fort Dearborn measurements are paces remembered, the payment of page 167 is dated to the wrong year, and the commanders' list is Hubbard's own search of the War Department records, which he says failed for the years after June 1833. The Winnebago Scare section (pages 166-174) is footnoted as coming not from the Diary but 'from statements by Mr. Hubbard in Chicago Historical Series, No. 10', which is one remove further.

transcribes.work: Caroline M. McIlvaine's Introduction, pages ix-xxvii — a 1911 review of the fifty-six years the Autobiography does not cover, compiled from letters, memoranda, contemporaries' reminiscences and printed history, and quoting E. O. Gale's Reminiscences of Early Chicago, The Chicago American of 10 October 1835, the Sunday Times of 24 October 1875 and Henry E. Hamilton's 1907 biographical sketch
transcribes.note: EVERY STATEMENT THIS PROJECT TAKES ABOUT 1834, 1835 OR 1836 COMES FROM HERE AND NOT FROM HUBBARD. The brick building at La Salle and South Water, the five or six hundred inhabitants, the brig Illinois of 25 May 1835, the Green Tree Tavern, the fire engine, the Russell & Mather purchase, the canal commissioners and the water-works are all McIlvaine's, written seventy-six years after the scene, and several are quotations at a further remove. A run reaching for 'Hubbard on 1835' is reaching for McIlvaine.

transcribes.work: Editorial notes by Henry E. Hamilton, signed H. E. H., inserted in square brackets in the narrative — including the note at page 178 that the hog-driving of 1829-30 'was the beginning of the packing industry in Chicago' — and the publishers' preface and closing note
transcribes.date: 1888 (the notes); 1911 (the preface and the closing note, the latter signed C. M. M.)
transcribes.note: Compiler's judgements, sixty years after the events, printed inside the narrative's own type. bk_hub_101 and bk_hub_104 are read from this layer and say so.

what_it_supplies: Fort Dearborn's occupation chronology, dated to the day, from its establishment in 1804 to its final abandonment on 29 December 1836 — which puts the scene year inside a continuous garrison running from 1 October 1832

a full description of the second fort as a man who lived beside it in 1818 remembered it: fourteen-foot oak pickets, a block house at the south-west corner and a bastion at the north-west, whitewashed stockade and buildings, the officers' quarters outside the pickets with a piazza at second-storey level, the soldiers' quarters, the sutler's store in the north-east corner, two gates, two ten-foot guardhouses, a two-storey commissary storehouse and a brick magazine

the fort's surroundings: a four-acre garden, a military barn, a field running half a mile south, the ONE road, a fence line closed from river to river, the well by the south gate, and wash-houses on the sandy beach east of the pickets

the Factor House — two storeys, squared logs, a split-picket fence, Jouett to about 1810 and then John Dean — and the American Fur Company's round-log storehouse built by John Craft and occupied after his death by Jean Baptiste Beaubien

John Kinzie's house described from inside it: a long log cabin with a rude piazza, fronting the river directly opposite the fort, with a window that had a sight-line to the fort at night — the piazza confirmed again nine years later

a complete building count for the whole of the present Cook County in 1818: the fort's group, the Factor House, the Fur Company storehouse, Hardscrabble, Ouilmette's cabin and Kinzie's house, and nothing else

the river mouth's history — its natural outlet at the fort, its southward migration behind a sand spit driven by north-east winds, its position at The Pines a mile south as late as 1827, the soldiers' cut of spring 1828 and the sand's refilling of it

landscape: the prairie seen from Douglas Grove, the Blue Island grove and the Desplaines timber, wild onion and leek along the river, wild rice and head-high grass at Mud Lake, the old cultivated field on the River Guarie still legible as cornhills, and prairie fires dangerous enough to sink boats against

Hubbard's Trail, dated by the man who cut it (1822 to Danville, extended north to Chicago in 1824) and the State road from Vincennes to Chicago ordered in the winter of 1833-34 that adopted most of it
the settlement's size taken sideways: about forty men and women turned out to fight the fort fire in 1827, and a majority of the men at the fort that summer were Hubbard's own employees

for 1835, at one remove through McIlvaine: the brig Illinois lightered ashore on 25 May because the harbour could not take her, the passengers going on to the Green Tree Tavern, the Chicago American of 10 October 1835 on Hubbard's fire engine, and the March 1835 purchase of the eighty acres of Russell & Mather's addition for $5,000
one period document, and it is graded separately: Hubbard's letter to his sister headed 'Chicago, July 25, 1827', at data/sources/hubbard_letter_1827_07_25.json
what_it_does_not_supply: Hubbard's own eyewitness on 1835. HIS NARRATIVE ENDS IN NOVEMBER 1830 and the closing note says so in as many words; the book's 1835 is Caroline McIlvaine's, written in 1911

any plat position, lot, or measured coordinate. Every placement here is prose — 'west and a little south of the fort', 'about where Wells street now crosses the river' — and several are given in streets that did not exist when the thing described did
reliable dimensions. 'A square of about six hundred feet' for the Fort Dearborn stockade is a pace-estimate at sixty years' distance and is much larger than the fort this project reconstructs

a consistent account of the officers' quarters: page 36 puts them outside the pickets and built of hewn logs, page 167 puts the commanding officers' former quarters in a brick building just within the north stockade and the log quarters within the pickets on the west. The book contradicts itself and this project does not resolve it
the right year for the Pottawatomie payment and the fort fire: page 167 prints 1828 where the section heading, the surrounding narrative and Hubbard's own dated letter all say July 1827
the names of the officers commanding Fort Dearborn after 19 June 1833 — Hubbard says he could not find them in the War Department records, so the source names nobody in command during the scene year
a residence for anybody in 1835. Every person Hubbard names, he names for what they did between 1812 and 1830
page images. This reading is of the Internet Archive's OCR text of the scan, corroborated against the deposited PDF's own text layer; no claim here is scan_verified
